candidate-models.t: Three classifiers have been scored on the **validation set**. Which one is best? That depends on **which question we care about**.

accuracy-view.t: By accuracy, **Model C** is best (**0.94**). But accuracy treats every mistake alike.

precision-view.t: By precision, Model C is again best (**0.95**): when it flags an email, it is almost always right.

recall-view.t: By recall the winner is **Model A (0.95)**, and Model C is the worst (**0.45**): it **misses more than half** of the positives.

f1-view.t: By F1, which balances precision and recall, **Model B** wins (**0.83**, against 0.81 for A and 0.61 for C). **Each metric crowns a different model.**

application-costs.t: **Spam filtering:** a false positive blocks legitimate mail, so precision matters. **Fraud screening:** a false negative is missed fraud, so recall matters. If both matter, **F1** is one balanced summary.

choose-metric.t: The order is: understand the **cost of each mistake**, pick the metric that reflects it, then compare models. Precision and F1 evaluate models; they are not automatically the training loss.

compare-validation.t: In fraud screening, where a person reviews flagged cases, **false alarms are cheap and missed fraud is costly**. Recall is the metric, and **Model A leads** on it.

select-model.t: We select **Model A** using **validation data only**. Model choice and hyperparameters are decided on validation data, never on the test set.

test-stays-locked.t: The test set is **scored once**, after the model and metric are final. If we picked the winner by test score, it would **stop being an honest estimate**.
